scenes.title: Where does this line hit the x-axis?
body: What must be true on the x-axis?
scenes.narration: Suppose a line is given by three x plus two y equals eighteen, and you are asked for its x-intercept. Here’s the idea: an intercept is not just a number you memorize how to find. It is a point where the graph meets an axis, so the geometry tells us what value must become zero.

scenes.title: The x-axis means y = 0
body: So for an x-intercept, set y = 0
Common mix-up: x = 0 finds the y-intercept
scenes.narration: Every point on the x-axis has y-coordinate zero. That is why finding an x-intercept means setting y equal to zero. This is where students often mix things up: setting x equal to zero finds the y-intercept, because points on the y-axis have x-coordinate zero.

scenes.title: Let the geometry simplify the algebra
scenes.narration: Now use the axis condition in the equation. Replace y with zero: three x plus two times zero equals eighteen. The y-term disappears, leaving three x equals eighteen. Notice why this works: we are restricting the equation to points that lie on the x-axis, then asking which of those points also lies on the line.

scenes.title: Solve, then write the POINT
body: Common mistake: writing only 6 when a point is requested
scenes.narration: Divide by three to get x equals six. But the x-intercept is the point six comma zero, not merely the number six, unless the question specifically asks only for the x-coordinate. That distinction matters on SAT-style questions.

scenes.title: Check the point in the original equation
body: Recap: axis condition first, algebra second
scenes.narration: Quick check: substitute six comma zero into the original equation. Three times six plus two times zero equals eighteen, so the point is on the line and on the x-axis. Recap the idea: the graph tells you the condition y equals zero, and that condition turns the two-variable equation into a one-variable equation you can solve. The full lesson is available on SUMMIT.
